title: Mendel's notebook of middot
hookLine: Mendel of Satanov turns Franklin's virtue notebook into a Mussar method
carry: one middah gets the whole week

lines: A BLACK MARK FOR EACH SLIP.
cards: Benjamin Franklin, in his autobiography, describes a small notebook. One page for each virtue he wanted. A column for each day of the week.
Each day he made a little black mark wherever he had slipped. He didn't try to fix everything at once.
He gave each virtue a week of close attention, then moved to the next, the way, he says, a gardener weeds one bed at a time instead of the whole garden.
A Jewish writer in Eastern Europe, Mendel of Satanov, read about that notebook.

teach.h: A TOOL BORROWED AND MADE HIS OWN.
teach.b: One trait a week. Four pieces. First, the borrowing.

Mendel of Satanov wrote a Hebrew book called Cheshbon HaNefesh, named for yesterday's word. In it he laid out a method for working on character that, as historians describe it, he adapted from Franklin's notebook.

teach.h: A LIST OF MIDDOT, EACH WITH A LINE.
teach.b: He chose his own list of traits, gave each a Hebrew name and a short line to carry, and wrote it for Jewish readers: a good tool, found in an unexpected place, put to work in his own house. Second, the list.
His traits are middot, measures, and several are coming in the days ahead: humility, patience, order, calm of soul, silence. Third, the week. Pick one trait.

teach.h: ONE TRAIT GETS THE WHOLE WEEK.
teach.b: For one week it gets your full attention: you say its short line, you watch for it during the day, and at night, in your accounting, you mark where it slipped.

teach.h: ONE, SO IT ACTUALLY SHOWS UP.
teach.b: The other traits aren't abandoned; they wait their turn.
The next week, the next trait. When the list is done, you go around again. Fourth, why one.
Try to become patient, humble, orderly and calm all by Friday, and it's easy to lose track of all four by Wednesday.
Give one trait seven days, the method hopes, and it starts to show up on its own, in the checkout line and the group chat. Mendel's gift was making it fit in a pocket: one page, one trait, one week.

how: In Mussar groups that follow Mendel of Satanov's Cheshbon HaNefesh, people focus on one trait for a week, repeat a short phrase for it, and note each evening where it slipped, then move to the next trait on the list.

games.q: you're a Jewish writer, and you've read about a statesman's notebook for working on virtues, one at a time. what do you do?
o: ignore it; it isn't from a Jewish book.
adapt it: your own list of middot, in Hebrew, for Jewish readers.
games.why: Mendel of Satanov made the method his own, with his own list of traits and a short line for each, in a book he named Cheshbon HaNefesh.

practice: Let a few traits pass through your mind, patience, honesty, order, calm, generosity, quiet, and choose the one this week actually needs.

Give it a short line of your own, a few plain words you could say at a red light, and picture one place this week where it will be tested, a meeting, a commute, a dinner, with the trait in your pocket.
If you pray, ask God's help with it in your own words; if not, simply hold the choice.

wordCard.voice: One trait a week. Mendel of Satanov's method, adapted from Benjamin Franklin's notebook: one middah gets a whole week of attention, with a short line and a nightly mark. Today's word.
